title: 25 States Sue Trump Administration for Tying Disaster Funds to Election Changes
excerpt: A coalition of mostly Democratic-led states filed suit in federal court to block DHS from withholding over $1 billion in FEMA grants unless states adopt election practices pushed by the administration.
body:
• 25 states and Washington, D.C. sued the Trump administration on Thursday to block DHS from withholding 20% of FEMA grant funding — at least $148 million — unless states adopt specific election practices.
  • The disputed policy, announced July 10, requires states to transition to hand-marked paper ballots, audit 5% of votes, and cross-check voter rolls against a DHS citizenship database to receive more than $1 billion in disaster-preparedness grants.
  • The lawsuit adds to a pattern of legal battles over federal funding conditions, following earlier suits over immigration enforcement requirements and the cancellation of the BRIC disaster mitigation program.

What Happened

A coalition of 25 mostly Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia filed a federal lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block the Department of Homeland Security from conditioning disaster-related funding on states' adoption of election administration practices favored by the Trump administration.

https://x.com/CurtisHouck/status/2080315533665214625

The suit, filed in federal court in Rhode Island and led by Rhode Island, California, Illinois and New Jersey, challenges a DHS policy announced on July 10 that withholds 20% of Federal Emergency Management Agency grant awards — more than $1 billion earmarked to help states prepare for terrorist attacks and other security threats — until states meet a set of election-related requirements.

"Congress never gave DHS or FEMA authority to rewrite state election law."

— Lawsuit complaint filed by the coalition of states

The Election Conditions

Under the disputed policy, states must submit plans to transition away from electronic voting systems that use bar codes and QR codes, switching instead to equipment that accepts hand-marked paper ballots. They must also conduct manual audits of at least 5% of all ballots cast in federal elections, reconcile the number of participating voters with the number of votes counted, and compare their voter registration rolls against a DHS database to verify no non-citizens are improperly registered.

DHS described the requirements as "common-sense steps to protect U.S. elections." A FEMA spokesperson said the new conditions would preserve election integrity, adding: "We fully expected these left-wing politicians to oppose common-sense measures designed to election security."

The states counter that none of the affected grant programs were designed with election security in mind and that the U.S. Constitution assigns states — not the federal government — the role of administering elections. States allocated more than $740 million in fiscal year 2026 stand to lose at least $148 million under the policy.

A Pattern of Funding Fights

The lawsuit is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and state governments over federal funding. In July 2025, 20 states sued DHS over the cancellation of the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program, a multibillion-dollar disaster mitigation initiative created during Trump's first term. A federal judge in Boston blocked that move in August 2025, preventing the diversion of more than $4 billion in grants.

Separately, in September 2025, a federal judge in Rhode Island ruled that the administration's effort to force states to cooperate with immigration enforcement as a condition for receiving billions in emergency and disaster aid was unlawful and unconstitutional.

The new suit escalates the conflict by directly linking disaster preparedness funding to election administration — a move critics say pushes the boundaries of federal authority further than previous attempts.

Midterms Backdrop

The filing comes ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections, where Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. The Trump administration has made election integrity a central issue, asserting that states are not doing enough to prevent voter fraud and voting by non-citizens. DHS recently sent letters to California, New Jersey, Nevada and Pennsylvania warning them of non-citizens on their voter rolls.

Independent studies and audits have consistently found voter fraud in U.S. elections to be rare. A Reuters analysis of federal court data published on July 19 found that many criminal cases involving non-citizen voting stemmed from voter confusion, miscommunication with election officials, or administrative errors rather than deliberate fraud.

However, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill acknowledged on Tuesday that more than 6,000 non-citizens had been accidentally registered to vote in the state and nearly 400 cast ballots, prompting demands from the Justice Department for data on those voters.

What's Next

The states are seeking a preliminary injunction to block the policy while the case proceeds. Given the pattern of judicial rulings against similar administration efforts — courts blocked both the BRIC cancellation and the immigration-enforcement funding conditions — legal experts will be watching whether the Rhode Island court follows suit.

The case is expected to move quickly given the proximity to the midterms and the immediate financial impact on states' disaster preparedness budgets. DHS and FEMA have not yet filed a formal response to the lawsuit.
nri_angle: Indian Americans in states affected by the funding dispute may see reduced disaster preparedness in their communities as federal grants face holdbacks tied to election policy battles.
